options: there is a difference or effect
there is no difference, relationship or effect, and any pattern is due to sampling variability
questions.why: We assume H₀ is true and ask how likely our sample result would be under it.

questions.q: A hypothesis test can lead us to...
options: reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis
accept the sample mean as the population mean
questions.why: Hypothesis testing never proves the alternative. We either reject H₀ or fail to reject it.

questions.q: When is a one-tailed test appropriate?
options: Whenever the result looks significant in one direction
Only when there's a clear reason, decided before looking at the data, to expect a difference in one direction
questions.why: Choosing a direction after seeing the data inflates the chance of a false positive.

how far the sample mean is from the null value, in units of standard error
questions.why: t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s / √n): the distance from what H₀ expects, scaled by the standard error.

if there were truly no difference, we'd see a difference at least this large in about 3% of random samples
there's a 97% chance the result is real
questions.why: The p-value assumes H₀ is true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and it says nothing about effect size.

questions.q: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true is a...
questions.why: The probability of a Type I error equals α, the significance level.

makes a Type I error more likely
questions.why: There's a trade-off. The main way to reduce both at once is a larger sample.

questions.q: Testing whether well water near a landfill is contaminated, which error could be most serious?
options: Type I: concluding there's contamination when there isn't
Type II: concluding there's no contamination when there is
Both are equally serious in every case
questions.why: Missing real contamination could harm people's health, so we might accept a higher chance of a Type I error.

questions.q: Why does running a LISA test for every county raise a concern about Type I errors?
options: With many tests at α = 0.05, some will be significant by chance alone
questions.why: Run 20 independent tests at 0.05 and you'd expect about one false positive.

questions.q: Comparing PM2.5 at the same monitors in 2019 and 2020 calls for...
questions.why: Each monitor is compared to itself, which removes differences between locations.

questions.q: Why use ANOVA instead of many t-tests to compare income across three NC regions?
options: Running many t-tests increases the chance of a Type I error
ANOVA tells you exactly which group differs
questions.why: A significant ANOVA says at least one mean differs. Post-hoc tests like Tukey's HSD find which one.

questions.q: Is commute mode related to whether a household is in an urban or rural tract? Which test fits?
questions.why: Both variables are categorical. The test compares observed counts in a contingency table to the counts expected under independence.

questions.q: If the expected frequency in some chi-square cells is below 5, you can use...
questions.why: Chi-square needs reasonably large expected counts in each cell.

questions.q: How does positive spatial autocorrelation affect a standard t-test?
options: Each observation carries less unique information than assumed, so standard errors are too small and p-values too low
questions.why: That raises the chance of a Type I error, which is one reason the course moves to spatial methods.

questions.q: With data for every US census tract, a $50 difference in median income is statistically significant. This shows that...
options: with very large samples, even tiny differences can be significant, so you should also report the effect size
questions.why: Significance depends heavily on sample size. Effect sizes and confidence intervals show whether a difference is big enough to matter.
